beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Reading what the agent says tells you nothing about whether it is safe, so you test it.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what is left, and what future sessions need before touching the system
beats.got: A list of verbs. Residual risk is at least a familiar term from telecom risk work.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I am meant to think about what to check before anyone relies on it. A fair question.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent's text becomes real actions, so a vague description or a bad context gives a bad action. That is concrete.

beats.trigger: Agent systems do not offer certainty.
beats.got: They admit up front that nobody can promise safety. That is rare in a vendor-style session.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Our security work assumes the same input gives the same output. That is sensible.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: A normal-looking document can steer the agent into misusing its access. This is not like the old security threats, and our people would not see it coming.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five standard controls, which is a risk register with new labels. Still usable.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: Admitting 'unknown' is acceptable, but it needs evidence behind it. We already do this in audits.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: Safe and useful pull against each other, and somebody has to sign for where the line is. I know that tension.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The cheapest safety measure is not connecting the thing at all, and that costs functionality. It is a plain statement of cost, with no sales pitch.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: It is complex and stays complex. True, but it reads like a closing line to me.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: A skill is a saved checklist the agent loads on demand. Fine.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent ran our policy files against the system I built and sorted rules into checkable and not. That is something I can test myself.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell the agent what matters here, and it should not give me boilerplate. Fair.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: A long interview. That is the part where my attention drifts.

beats.trigger: Answer what you can briefly, then hand back the rest: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: I answer what I know and let the agent decide the rest. Efficient, though I am not sure I trust that.

beats.trigger: The skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: Install steps. Nothing to react to.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The agent check is an addition to our existing controls. That is what our security people would want to hear.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: They do not promise a clean result. I will see what I get.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Checking that the tool is there.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit found rows I had assumed were fine and marked them 'can't tell'. That is more honest than a green tick, and I could read the report myself.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The ranked risks make me uneasy and I am told to treat that as a signal. A bit neat as a line, but the risks were real.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: I applied one fix, the risk is still there, and I wrote it down and accepted it. That is how risk work normally goes.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report.
beats.got: When it is beyond me, I take the report and a narrow question to legal or security. Sensible, and it keeps humans responsible.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: One risk was a demo. A real agent needs this for every risk, which is a lot of work.

beats.trigger: Certainty is not on offer.
beats.got: I ended with reports and a recorded decision, not a guarantee.

beats.trigger: Read the agent's summary and push back where it's wrong
beats.got: The agent writes rules for next time and I correct them. Reasonable.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills can be shared with colleagues, but they do not decide who owns what. Fair caveat.

beats.trigger: Well-formed English is the attack surface, even via sources.
beats.got: Ordinary text in a document can be the attack. That is the point I will remember.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework for the next module. I will decide later.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases to read where someone failed to check AI output. Real cases are more convincing than slides.

take_homes: A normal document the agent reads can steer it into misusing access it already has, so the text itself is the attack surface.
Nobody can promise an agent is safe. You run a check, apply one fix, write down the residual risk and have someone sign for it.
The cheapest safety measure is leaving a door unopened, and that costs a feature.

monday.move: Nothing on Monday. If a pilot is proposed I would ask for the two-lens audit report on it before anyone signs off.
monday.who: Me, then our security and legal people if a pilot comes up
monday.when: Only when a concrete pilot exists
monday.stop_condition: No audit report, or a report with unexplained 'can't tell' rows
monday.blocker: Steering-group calendar, and I would rather wait to see what the pilots show

misconception.why: This is a risk I can see is real and different from earlier waves: ordinary text steering an agent that has access. It was shown on a system I built, and the 'we cannot give certainty' framing is not a sales pitch. I still think many agent projects will fizzle, but I no longer think I can ignore this one.

one_line: Unusually honest for a training: it says outright you can't be certain, and the audit gives you a report you can check yourself, but the middle is a lot of fiddling with skill files.
